Project: Case Numbers 37-25CUP – 1768 Arrow Highway, Suite 102 – Conditional Use
Permit to operate a holistic health and wellness center located at 1768 Arrow Highway.
The property has a zoning designation of Arrow Corridor Specific Plan and the property
lies within the Commercial/Manufacturing (C/M) area which requires approval of a
Conditional Use Permit for health spas

RECOMMENDATION:
Staff recommends that the Planning Commission do one of the following:
  1. Approve the project and direct staff to return at the next meeting with a resolution
  approving the project based on appropriate findings, with or without conditions or
  modifications deemed appropriate and affirm a categorical exemption from the
  California Environmental Act; or
  2. Continue the public hearing to a date certain to allow for further analysis or revisions;
  or
  3. Deny the project and direct staff to return at the next meeting with a resolution denying
  the project based on appropriate findings.

Regardless of whether the Planning Commission approves or denies the project, it should
provide its reasoning to staff for its decision so that the appropriate findings can be made and
incorporated into a resolution.
 Presentation: Associate Planner Stringfellow made a presentation to the Planning Commission
going over the recommendations and staff report.

Public Hearing: Vice-Chairperson Allison opened the public hearing. The applicant Priscilla
Ortiz was present at the meeting. Ms. Ortiz shared her background. She stated that she
previously operated her business for ten years in the City of Upland. Ms. Ortiz was unaware of
the steps to open her business in La Verne. She is currently referral based only and travels to
the homes of her clients while she prepares to open the new space. Ms. Ortiz provided photos of
the space for the Commissioners and Staff.

The Commissioners had questions regarding state licensing and the Upland location.

Ms. Ortiz stated that she has certifications for some of the services but there are no state
licensing requirements for the services she is providing. Ms. Ortiz also stated that she has a
seller’s permit and applied for business license. She began her setup of the space in 2022,
setting up one room at a time but has not opened to the public.

Vice-Chairperson Allison closed the public hearing.

Commissioner Discussion: The Commissioners asked for clarification regarding difference
between a massage CUP and health spa CUP.

Mr. Stringfellow stated that the massage service is less than 20%. Mr. Scherer added that the
massage service is ancillary to the health spa and any future business in the space would have
to follow the same conditions.

Commissioner Chang asked if more conditions can be added to the CUP.

Mr. Scherer stated that more conditions can be added at the Commissioners request and be
brought back to the next meeting. He added that the CUP is still revocable if conditions are not
met or followed.

Vice-Chairperson Allison reopened the Public Hearing and asked Ms. Ortiz if she was aware of
the complaints received by the City.

Ms. Ortiz was surprised by the complaints as she had never received hate from others or
complaints before.

Vice-Chairperson Allison closed the Public Hearing.

The Commissioners discussed the highlighted conditions in the staff report. Mr. Scherer stated
that he felt the highlighted conditions were appropriate for the business.

It was moved by Commissioner Conrad and seconded by Commissioner Duffy to return a
resolution for approval at the next regularly scheduled meeting, approving the project based on
the findings being met as set forth in the staff report, with the draft conditions of approval and
affirm a categorical exemption from the California Environmental Act. Motion carried by a 4-0
vote.

SUMMARY
Four ordinances are being presented for Planning Commission recommendation to
bring the La Verne Municipal Code into compliance with State law and implement the
General Plan. Updates address accessory dwelling units (ADUs), historic structures and
noise regulations, reasonable accommodations, and two-unit housing projects and
urban lot splits. All actions are exempt from CEQA or covered by prior environmental
review.

While this staff report covers all four ordinances, the Commission should have a
separate hearing on each item.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends the Planning Commission recommend approval of each of these
ordinancesto the City Council by adoption of the attached resolutions for each draft
ordinance.

DISCUSSION
The proposed ordinances amend several sections of the La Verne Municipal Code to
ensure compliance with State mandates and to implement policies from the City's
updated General Plan. A summary of each ordinance and its proposed changes is
outlined below:

  1. Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) and Junior ADUs:
  This ordinance updates the City’s ADU and JADU regulations to align with

  current State law. The Ordinance has been redlined against current provisions
  so changes are easily identifiable. Not all sections have changes, but they are
  included in the Ordinance without change so the provisions can be reviewed in
  their totality. Key changes include:
  o Incorporation of definitions included in the State ADU law, either directly or
  by reference.
  o Revised permit processing procedures to meet State requirements.
  o Clarification of allowable ADU locations and the number of units permitted
  per lot.
  o Updated development standards, including height limits and parking
  requirements.
  o Provisions regarding the treatment of units constructed prior to January 1,
  2020, even if unpermitted.
  o Additional protections for properties subject to a Mills Act contract,
  recognizing their historic significance.These updates are intended to
  expand housing options while ensuring responsible integration into
  existing neighborhoods.

  The ADU/JADU Ordinance is exempt from CEQA pursuant to Public Resoruces
  Code section 21080.17 which provides CEQA does not apply to ordinances
  implementing the ADU law.

  2. Historic Structures and Noise Ordinance:
  The recently adopted General Plan Update included a number of actions to be
  taken as follow-up. Two actions relate to historic structures and noise.

  Historic Structures:
  A new section is added to preserve and regulate historic structures. The
  ordinance restricts demolition or significant alteration of historic buildings
  damaged by natural disasters unless:
  o The work restores or enhances the structure’s historic value;
  o The Building Official determines the structure poses an imminent safety
  hazard; or
  o The State Office of Historic Preservation authorizes demolition or
  alteration under the Public Resources Code.

  Noise Regulations:
  Chapter 8.20 is repealed and readopted to reflect updated noise policies
  consistent with the General Plan. Key updates include:
  o Clearly defined noise limits by property type and time of day.
  o Requirements for construction noise management plans near residential
  areas.
  o New standards for vibration impacts and mobile equipment.
  o Revised exemptions for certain activities such as emergencies and minor
  home maintenance.

  o  Enhanced enforcement measures, including provisions for repeat police
  responses to loud parties.

  The environmental impacts of this Ordinance were analyzed under the EIR for
  the General Plan.

  3. Reasonable Accommodation:
  This ordinance repeals and replaces Chapter 18.116 to bring the City's
  reasonable accommodation procedures into compliance with State and federal
  fair housing laws. Revising the reasonable accommodation provisions was one
  of the programs in the City’s 2021-2029 Housing Element. The proposed
  ordinance is modeled on the City of Oakland’s ordinance, whose initial draft was
  revised in response to concerns raised by a disability advocacy agency for
  people with disabilities. Key features include:
  o A formal process for individuals with disabilities to request flexibility in
  zoning and building regulations.
  o Clear definitions for applicants, disabilities, and types of accommodations.
  o Application procedures, including a 30-day review timeline and required
  findings.
  o Privacy protections, application assistance, and a formal appeal process.
  o Applicability to both standalone requests and those tied to other land use
  permits.

  This Ordinance is categorically exempt from CEQA pursuant to the common sense
  exemption set forth in Guidelines section 15061(b)(3) that CEQA only applies to projects
  which have the potential for causing a significant effect on the environment and where it
  can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the activity will have a
  significant effect, the activity is not subject to CEQA.

  4. Two-Unit Housing Projects and Urban Lot Splits (SB 9):
  This ordinance introduces minor but important updates to LVMC § 16.12.060 and
  Chapter 18.122 to comply with recent changes in state law to SB 9. The
  Ordinance has been redlined against current provisions so changes are easily
  identifiable. Proposed changes include:
  o A 60-day time limit for the City to act on two-unit and urban lot split
  applications.
  o Clarification of the number of units allowed when no lot split occurs.
  o Identification of additional site types where such development is
  prohibited.
  o A requirement that only objective standards may be applied to these
  projects.

  This Ordinance is exempt from CEQA pursuant to Government Code sections
  65852.21 and 66411.7 which provides that ordinances implementing SB 9 are
  exempt from CEQA.

SUMMARY
The applicant, Priscilla Ortiz of Tree of Life Botanicals has submitted an application for a
Conditional Use Permit to operate a holistic health and wellness center located at 1768
Arrow Highway. The property has a zoning designation of Arrow Corridor Specific Plan
and the property lies within the Commercial/Manufacturing (C/M) area which requires
approval of a Conditional Use Permit for health spas.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the Planning Commission do one of the following:

  1. Approve the project and direct staff to return at the next meeting with a resolution
  approving the project based on appropriate findings, with or without conditions or
  modifications deemed appropriate and affirm a categorical exemption from the
  California Environmental Quality Act; or

  2. Continue the public hearing to a date certain to allow for further analysis or
  revisions; or

  3. Deny the project and direct staff to return at the next meeting with a resolution
  denying the project based on appropriate findings.

Regardless of whether the Planning Commission approves or denies the project, it
should provide its reasoning to staff for its decision so that the appropriate findings can
be made and incorporated into a resolution.

PARKING
The proposed business will utilize the commercial center’s shared parking lot.
Consistent with AB 2097 which was adopted by the State Legislature in 2022, parking
cannot be required for the approval of new commercial business development when the
development is within one-half mile from transit, which this proposed location is.

For the information of the commission, per the LVMC, health spas require one parking
space per every 150 square foot of gross floor area, which would require 15 parking
spaces for the 2,200 square foot business. The applicant is proposing workshops and
seminars for 10-15 people on Saturday mornings or afternoons once a month.
Educational facilities require one parking space per employee plus one space for every
three students, plus parking for public assembly areas at either one space for every
three seats, or one space per 30 square feet of assembly area where there are no fixed
seats. Per the proposed operation of workshops or seminars with no more than five
participants and one employee, there would be no more than 6 parking spaces required.
As Saturday is not typically a business day for office-type land uses, the shared parking
lot demand will be lower than during the week, allowing more spaces to be open for
workshop participants.

COMPATIBILITY WITH SURROUNDING USES
Health spas are located throughout La Verne and are allowed in the Arrow Corridor
Specific Plan Commercial/Manufacturing zone if a Conditional Use Permit is secured.
Most of the surrounding land uses are commercial or industrial, including some office
uses within the same commercial building. Across Arrow Highway to the north are the
LA Metro A-line tracks, with residential north of the tracks. The adjacent property to the
west contains a property management company, and across A Street to the east is an
auto repair shop. Directly adjacent to the south is a parking lot owned by the University
of La Verne and utilized by Gilead Sciences Inc. employees. Staff does not expect that
the normal operation of the business will negatively affect the surrounding businesses
and land uses.

CONDITIONAL USE PERMIT FINDINGS
To approve a conditional use, the Planning Commission must make the five findings set
forth in La Verne Municipal Code section 18.108.030B; there are no special
requirements for this type of use. Staff is providing their advice to the commission in the
discussions of each of the findings below .

  1. The proposed use and development are each consistent with the general plan
  and the applicable land use zone.

Discussion: The proposed use is consistent with the general plan land use designation
which is Specific Plan – Mixed Use, which refers to areas implemented with Specific
Plans which allow for a mix of land uses, including commercial. The
Commercial/Manufacturing designation within the Arrow Corridor Specific Plan zone
allows health spas, a type of commercial land use, with a Conditional Use Permit.
Therefore, the proposed holistic health and wellness center is a use that is consistent
with the general plan and land use designation.
  2. The site for the proposed use is adequate in size, shape, topography,
  accessibility, and other physical characteristics to accommodate the proposed
  use and development in a manner compatible with existing and proposed
  surrounding land uses.

Discussion: The use is being proposed in an existing building in a location which has
been used for a variety of different uses over the past two decades. Staff has reviewed
the proposal and are advising that the site is adequate in size, shape, topography,
accessibility and other physical characteristics to accommodate the proposed business,
that current businesses in the center include various office uses which are compatible
with the proposed business, and that the proposed business is not expected to cause
noise or other disturbances nor negatively impact surrounding businesses or the
nearest residential land uses due to its normal operation.
  3. The development site has adequate access to those utilities and other services
  required or the proposed use.

Discussion: All required utilities and other services required for the proposed use
already exist on the property and are accessible by the proposed business. No new
utilities or services will be required.
